implementation_notes: The command is any callable - a bound method, a lambda, or a `functools.partial` that binds a receiver and its arguments - which replaces the Command subclass hierarchy. `queue.Queue(maxsize=N)` is the repository: `put` blocks when full, so the bound is real backpressure, and `ThreadPoolExecutor` is the executor whose `submit()` returns the `Future` that the history/log layer records and that surfaces exceptions. Undo is a list of inverse callables pushed by each command. The classic class structure starts earning its keep when commands must be persisted, validated or replayed (Celery/dramatiq-style durable queues) or when the request needs attributes beyond its arguments.
code_sketch:
q: "queue.Queue[Callable[[], None]]" = queue.Queue(maxsize=256)   # bounded
history: list[Callable[[], None]] = []
with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    while (cmd := q.get()) is not None:
        fut = pool.submit(cmd)        # executor owns when/where it runs
        fut.add_done_callback(lambda f: history.append(cmd))   # log / undo
        q.task_done()
q.put(partial(service.place_order, order_id, qty))          # invocation only
pitfalls: An exception raised inside a submitted callable is stored in the Future and invisible unless it is inspected (`fut.exception()`/done_callback); the processor must record failures explicitly.
queue.Queue.join() hangs forever if any error path skips task_done(); wrap execution in try/finally.
Queue() with no maxsize is unbounded - producers never slow down and memory grows under load.
The GIL means CPU-bound commands gain nothing from more workers; use ProcessPoolExecutor (which requires picklable commands and payloads) for CPU work.

variants.name: asyncio.Queue + worker task (single-threaded async)
variants.idiom_name: async command coroutines + asyncio.Queue + create_task worker loop
variants.implementation_notes: In an async application the repository is `asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N)` (`await queue.put()` blocks the producer coroutine when full) and the executor is one or more `asyncio.create_task(...)` workers awaiting `queue.get()`; commands are async callables, so I/O-bound receivers run concurrently on one thread without locks, and ordering is deterministic when a single worker drains the queue. Mixed applications should keep one repository, not two: blocking callables go to `loop.run_in_executor`/a thread pool from inside the async worker via `asyncio.to_thread`, rather than a second queue.
variants.code_sketch:
queue: asyncio.Queue[Callable[[], Awaitable[None]]] = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=256)
async def processor() -> None:                # one worker == deterministic order
    while True:
        cmd = await queue.get()
        try:
            history.append(cmd)               # log / undo
            await cmd()                       # async command body
        finally:
            queue.task_done()
worker = asyncio.create_task(processor())
await queue.put(place_order(order_id, qty))    # suspends when full == backpressure
pitfalls: A blocking call inside the worker (requests, time.sleep, sync DB driver) freezes the whole event loop; offload it with asyncio.to_thread.
asyncio.Queue is not thread-safe: producers on other threads must use loop.call_soon_threadsafe, not queue.put_nowait.
A worker task that raises ends silently unless awaited or wrapped; the processor loop must catch per command and keep draining.
Abandoning the worker task at shutdown leaves queued commands unexecuted - cancel the task and drain the queue (or await queue.join()) explicitly.
